new.text: Kongzi, in one of his only recorded sayings about women: “Women and servants are {{c1::most difficult to nurture}}. If one is close to them, {{c2::they lose their reserve}}, while if one is distant, {{c3::they feel resentful}}.”

new.front: Until which dynasty was there almost no discussion of what a Confucian ethic for women might be?
new.back: The Han (206 BCE – 220 CE)

new.front: Why do some say Confucianism is for men and Daoism for women?
new.back: Confucianism means actively cultivating oneself and changing things for the better — the masculine yang. Daoism urges passively following the way of nature, in harmony with it — the feminine yin.

new.front: How did Ban Zhao come to be a court historian?
new.back: She took up the mantle after her father, Ban Biao, and her brother, Ban Gu, died — and finished the history of the Han they had begun

new.front: What makes Ban Zhao rare in Chinese literature?
new.back: She is one of very few women who both wrote and had their writing preserved

new.front: When did Zhu Xi live, relative to Kongzi?
new.back: More than 1,500 years later: Zhu Xi lived 1130–1200 CE, Kongzi 551–479 BCE

new.front: What was the religious climate when Zhu Xi was born, and what did he set out to do?
new.back: Buddhism was very strong; he wanted to turn the focus back to Confucianism

new.front: What system did Zhu Xi devise to put Neo-Confucian philosophy into practice?
new.back: Granaries kept full even in famine — eventually a statewide system. The greatest ren is to care for people.

new.text: The five relationships Neo-Confucianism made the foundation of a well-ordered society: four hierarchical — {{c1::father–son}}, {{c2::lord–servant}}, {{c3::husband–wife}} and {{c4::older brother–younger brother}} — and one equal, friend–friend
new.extra: The list goes back to Mengzi (3A4).

new.front: What became paramount for women under Neo-Confucianism?
new.back: Female chastity — and with it, footbinding

new.front: Where did Zhu Xi stand on whether human nature is good?
new.back: With Mengzi: human nature is principle (li), and so good; evil comes from the material force (qi) that clouds it

new.front: What was footbinding?
new.back: Breaking a young girl's feet — at three to five years old — folding the toes under, and binding them tightly so the feet looked extremely small

new.front: How is footbinding said to have begun?
new.back: In the 10th century, a ruler of the Southern Tang had his concubine bind her feet to perform a dance

new.front: How did footbinding spread?
new.back: By the Song dynasty, prostitutes, dancers and other female entertainers had taken it up; from them it spread to the upper classes

new.front: Why was footbinding seen as serving chastity?
new.back: A woman with bound feet couldn't easily leave the house

new.front: In a society that counted being born a woman a misfortune, how could footbinding turn it to advantage?
new.back: Bound feet could let a girl marry into the upper classes — a path to social mobility

new.front: Who, by tradition, wrote the Daodejing, and when did he live?
new.back: Laozi — an older contemporary of Kongzi

new.front: What do contemporary scholars say about Laozi and the Daodejing?
new.back: Laozi is a mythical figure, and the text is a composite work

new.front: Though the Daodejing was cobbled together from many sources, how does it read?
new.back: As if it was put together in a fairly short time, possibly by a single editor

new.front: How many chapters does the Daodejing have, and what are they like?
new.back: 81 — short passages, some of which rhyme

new.front: What does the title “Daodejing” mean?
new.back: “The Classic of Dao and De” — of the Way and Virtue

new.front: Where does the Daodejing get its title?
new.back: From the first concept of each of its two books, not from their content: Book I (chapters 1–37) is the Dao half, and Book II (38–81) the De half

new.front: When was the Daodejing put together, and how does it respond to its times?
new.back: Near the end of the Warring States period, an age of interstate rivalry. Weary of war and chaos, it longs for security and peace.

new.front: What does the Daodejing trace wars of expansion and corrupt government to?
new.back: Greed and ambition — hence its view that desire must be limited if it isn't to cause harm

new.front: What earlier time does the Daodejing appeal to?
new.back: A time when goodness was reflexive and instinctive, not thought out

new.front: What place do human beings have in the Dao?
new.back: A place, but not an exalted one: they are one kind of thing among others

new.front: Why do human beings upset the harmony of the Dao, and what does the Daodejing seek to do about it?
new.back: They can alter the nature of things, so they tend to forsake their natural place. The text seeks to undo this.

new.front: What kind of text does the introduction call the Daodejing, rather than a presentation of theory?
new.back: Philosophical therapy

new.front: How do opposites relate, according to the Daodejing?
new.back: They harmonise with and offset each other (ch. 2)

new.text: The Daodejing: revering important people leads to {{c1::strife}}; revering material possessions leads to {{c2::theft}}

new.front: Where does the Daodejing mention a lord or god, and in what context?
new.back: Only once, in chapter 4: the Dao is “the image of what was before the Lord himself”

new.front: Who is the “Enigmatic Female” in the Daodejing?
new.back: The spirit of the valley — her gate is the root of Heaven and earth (ch. 6)

new.front: What paradox does the Daodejing see in the sages?
new.back: They put themselves last, yet come first; having no thought of themselves, they are able to perfect themselves (ch. 7)

new.text: The Daodejing on where the good lies: “In a residence, the good lies in {{c1::location}}. In hearts, the good lies in {{c1::depth}}. In interactions with others, the good lies in {{c2::benevolence}}. In words, the good lies in {{c2::trustworthiness}}. In government, the good lies in {{c3::orderliness}}. In carrying out one's business, the good lies in {{c3::ability}}. In actions, the good lies in {{c4::timeliness}}. Only by {{c4::avoiding contention}} can one avoid blame.”

new.front: What does the Daodejing say comes of being haughty about one's prestige and wealth?
new.back: One brings disaster on oneself (ch. 9)

new.front: How does the Daodejing want a ruler to lead?
new.back: Caring for the people and ordering the state, but without lording it over them (ch. 10)

new.front: What is the point of the Daodejing's clay vessel and room?
new.back: What's useful is what's absent: we shape clay into a vessel but use its cavity, and doors, walls and windows make a room but we use the space they leave (ch. 11)

new.front: What does the Daodejing say constant chasing and hunting do to us?
new.back: They madden our hearts (ch. 12)

new.front: In the Daodejing, what does revering and caring for your own body show?
new.back: That you're worthy of being trusted with more responsibility (ch. 13, which says to “revere calamity as you revere your own body”)

new.front: What does the Daodejing say stillness does to muddy water?
new.back: Makes it clear — where movement stirs up what was still (ch. 15)

new.front: What does the Daodejing keep urging a return to?
new.back: A better, more natural state

new.front: Which ruler does the Daodejing rank above one who is loved and praised?
new.back: One who is “but a shadowy presence” — and a loved ruler is better than one who is feared and reviled (ch. 17)

new.front: What paradox about loss and gain does the Daodejing draw?
new.back: As more can lead to less, so less can yield more: good comes out of bad circumstances (ch. 22)

new.front: What does the Daodejing repeatedly say comes of abandoning something good?
new.back: Something good — overthinking, it seems, gets in the way of goodness

new.front: When, according to the Daodejing, do virtues become noticeable?
new.back: Only when something has gone wrong — filial piety shows when families are at odds, loyal ministers when the state is in chaos (ch. 18)

new.front: When the Daodejing's author shifts into the first person, what do they say of themselves and the common folk?
new.back: That they are at a loss, while the common folk are “bright and brilliant” (ch. 20)

new.front: What does the Daodejing say bragging and self-aggrandisement lead to?
new.back: People not liking you (ch. 24)

new.front: What does the Way model itself on, according to the Daodejing?
new.back: What is natural. Humans model themselves on Earth, Earth on Heaven, and Heaven on the Way (ch. 25).

new.front: What does the Daodejing say of those who are truly good at something — and so of sages?
new.back: They make no mistakes and need no crutches; so sages save people and never abandon anyone (ch. 27)

new.front: Which line of the Daodejing counsels holding to the feminine?
new.back: “Know the male but preserve the female” (ch. 28)

new.front: What does the Daodejing say comes of taking the world by force of arms?
new.back: It comes back in kind (ch. 30)

new.front: What is the Daodejing's stance on weapons?
new.back: All creatures find them repulsive, so one who is on the Way doesn't rely on them — but may use them when there is no choice (ch. 31)

new.front: What does the Daodejing say of reveling in victory?
new.back: It is reveling in the slaughter of human beings, and one who delights in that won't achieve his ambitions (ch. 31)

new.front: What does the Daodejing say about striving for virtue?
new.back: It isn't how you gain virtue (ch. 38)

new.front: What does the stability of Heaven and earth show, according to the Daodejing?
new.back: That they have “attained the One” — so they don't tear themselves apart (ch. 39)

new.front: What does the Daodejing say about how the Way appears?
new.back: It may not seem level, or to lead forward, but it is — and only the Way is good at providing and completing (ch. 41)

new.front: How does everything arise from the Way, according to the Daodejing?
new.back: The Way produces the One, its representation; the One produces the two, yin and yang; the two produce the three; and the three produce everything in the world (ch. 42)

new.front: What kind of process is the Daodejing's account of how everything arises from the Way?
new.back: A natural progression, with no creator or higher power

new.text: The Daodejing: “Know {{c1::contentment}} and avoid disgrace; know {{c2::when to stop}} and avoid danger; and you will {{c3::long endure}}”

new.front: Whom is the Daodejing's sage good to, and whom does he trust?
new.back: The good and the bad alike; the trustworthy and those who aren't, alike (ch. 49)

new.front: What does the Daodejing say understanding the world and its source allows?
new.back: Avoiding danger (ch. 52) — the source being the Way, or the One

new.front: What does the Daodejing call strength?
new.back: Preserving the weak (ch. 52)

new.front: What does the Daodejing call possessing wealth in gross abundance while the granaries are empty?
new.back: Taking pride in robbery (ch. 53)

new.front: When does the Daodejing say to put things in order?
new.back: Before they become disordered — preparing is easy while things are going well (ch. 64)

new.front: What does the Daodejing say of those good at fighting, and of generals?
new.back: They aren't overly aggressive and don't start fights; generals don't want to make the first move (ch. 68–69)

new.front: What question does the Daodejing say even sages find difficult?
new.back: Why Heaven dislikes what it does (ch. 73)

new.front: What lesson does the Daodejing draw from water's suppleness?
new.back: The weak overcome the strong: nothing is more supple or weak than water, yet nothing can surpass it or resist its advance (ch. 78)

new.text: The Daodejing's ideal people {{c1::use no labour-saving tools, ships or carts}}, {{c2::keep track with knots instead of writing}} and {{c3::don't travel}} — yet {{c4::their food is savoury, their clothes fine, their houses comfortable and their lives happy}}

new.front: What do some scholars think “Laozi” was, if not one man?
new.back: A name taken by a group of people — some even think a group of women

new.front: Why do some think a group of women may have taken the name Laozi?
new.back: Women weren't allowed to be philosophers, and Daoism values qualities Chinese culture held inferior — women among them

new.front: How does the theory that Laozi was a group fit Daoist thought?
new.back: It fits the Daoist idea that no one person is above the rest

new.front: What does “Daoism” literally translate as?
new.back: “Way-ism” — dao means “way”

new.front: How does the Daodejing's style differ from the Analects'?
new.back: The Analects is straightforward and conversational; the Daodejing is cryptic, poetic and opaque

new.front: Why is the Daodejing full of repeated sounds?
new.back: To break you away from everyday thinking

new.front: Besides its key concepts, what two things does Daoism distrust?
new.back: Words — it is wary of language as an expression of the Truth, or the Way — and society. Both can lead people astray.

new.front: If words fail to express the Way, what does Daoism turn to?
new.back: The yin and the yang

new.front: What is the Way, in Daoism?
new.back: A cosmic force, or the natural order — the ideal state and the root of all things. Human beings should live in harmony with it.

new.text: What the yin-yang picture teaches: {{c1::all things are equal}}; {{c2::life is constant flux}}; {{c3::pushing to one extreme brings its opposite}}; {{c4::each thing holds the seed of its opposite}}; and {{c5::evil is imbalance, not the dark half}}

new.front: What does the equal size of the yin-yang's halves teach?
new.back: That things are equal — neither half is higher, and both are needed to make an integrated whole, even things you might not prefer in this life

new.front: What does it mean that each half of the yin-yang is moving into the other?
new.back: Nothing is static: life is a constant flux, a balancing out of two opposites

new.front: What does the yin-yang teach where each side grows thickest, just as it turns into the other?
new.back: Push too far to one extreme and you get its opposite

new.front: What does the dot of the other colour in each half of the yin-yang teach?
new.back: The seeds of each thing's opposite exist within it

new.front: If the yin-yang's white and dark halves aren't good and evil, what is true evil in Daoism?
new.back: The imbalance of the two sides

new.meaning: “non-action” — avoiding purposeful action; one of Daoism's main concepts, stressed again and again in the Daodejing

new.text: The lecture's illustration of wuwei, from the Daodejing: “Everyone knows that when the beautiful strives to be beautiful, {{c1::it is repulsive}}. Everyone knows that when good strives to be good, {{c2::it is no good}}.”
new.extra: Chapter 2. Self-conscious striving to excel at something good is counterproductive.

new.front: Why does Daoism counsel against purposeful action?
new.back: Trying to attain something leads to grief — harm comes from pushing too hard toward a goal. We naturally, unconsciously strive for a middle path, and avoiding purposeful action is how to reach it.

new.front: How, in Daoism, do you work out what to do?
new.back: Passively emulate the natural order: first observe nature and your surroundings; once you've worked out their natural order, act in harmony with it, avoiding extremes

new.front: Why is water the Daodejing's example of the highest good, and a key Daoist symbol?
new.back: Water benefits everything without causing harm or strife, and doesn't avoid what people think inferior — it shows how to live in accordance with the Way (ch. 8)

new.front: Where do Daoism and Confucianism each find the way to harmony and peace?
new.back: Daoism: in the individual's place within the cosmos, the natural order. Confucianism: in appropriate human relationships within the social order — for it, the only order worth following.

new.front: Why does Daoism say society's rules should not always be followed?
new.back: Society often puts the individual in opposition to the natural order

new.front: What does Confucianism say people must do, and how should it be rewarded?
new.back: Actively cultivate themselves — and be rewarded with important positions in government

new.front: Why does Daoism reject the Confucian call to self-cultivation?
new.back: Actively pursuing a goal brings about its opposite: rewarding self-cultivation makes people fight among themselves for the rewards, ending in chaos, strife and ignorance

wrel-190.back: Zhu Xi, arguably — he drew together the work of earlier Song-dynasty thinkers. It was a revival of Confucianism after a decline.
